## In Plain English

This case is about whether a court can punish Apple for disobeying a court order when the order did not clearly say the specific conduct was forbidden. The Supreme Court agreed to review one main issue: whether civil contempt — a court’s power to punish someone for violating a court order — requires the order to clearly and unambiguously prohibit the exact conduct, or whether a court can also rely on the order’s broader purpose or “spirit.” Regular people may care because the decision could affect how courts police large technology companies, how clearly court orders must be written, and how much room companies have to change their practices after being ordered to stop certain conduct.

## The Backstory

Epic Games, Inc. sued Apple Inc. in a federal trial court in the Northern District of California, case number 4:20-cv-5640. The dispute involves Apple’s App Store and rules about how people buy digital goods through apps.

According to Apple’s petition to the Supreme Court, Epic challenged the framework governing the global distribution of mobile applications. The latest round of litigation concerns whether Apple could be held in civil contempt for charging a commission on “link-out purchases.” A link-out purchase is a purchase of digital goods through an app running on Apple’s operating system and downloaded from the App Store, but completed outside the app through a third-party payment system.

Apple’s petition says the district court had earlier issued a permanent injunction. An injunction is a court order requiring someone to do something or stop doing something. Apple says the Ninth Circuit — the federal appeals court that reviewed the case — recognized that the text of the district court’s original injunction “does not address commissions at all,” but still affirmed a contempt finding based on the idea that parties may be held in contempt for violating the “spirit” of an injunction.

Epic’s Supreme Court brief describes the background differently. It says Apple required purchases of digital content through iPhone apps to use Apple’s own payment system, where Apple charged a 30% commission, and prohibited app developers from linking users to other payment systems or telling users those options existed. Epic says the district court enjoined those “anti-steering” practices, meaning Apple could not prohibit developers from linking users to other payment systems or from telling users that other options exist. Epic says Apple then imposed a commission on linked-out purchases and design restrictions that had the same purpose and effect as the old rules.

The case reached the Supreme Court after Apple filed a petition for a writ of certiorari on May 21, 2026. A petition for a writ of certiorari is a request asking the Supreme Court to review a lower court’s decision. Apple asked the Court to decide two questions. The Supreme Court granted review on June 30, 2026, but limited the case to Question 1. That means the Court agreed to decide only the first issue: the standard for civil contempt. Apple’s second question concerned whether the Ninth Circuit had created an exception to limits on broad injunctions under a Supreme Court case called Trump v. CASA, Inc. The provided docket shows that question was not granted for review.

Before the Supreme Court decided whether to hear the case, Apple filed a waiver of the 14-day waiting period for distribution of the petition on June 5, 2026. A waiver is a request to skip a normal waiting period. Apple said the parties had agreed to an expedited briefing schedule so the Court could consider the petition at its June 25 conference. A conference is a meeting where the Justices consider whether to hear a case. The docket shows the case was distributed for conference on June 9 and June 29, 2026.

During the case, Apple also asked for a stay. A stay is an order pausing lower-court proceedings. On August 12, 2026, Apple filed an application for a stay, submitted to Justice Kagan. Justice Kagan entered an order administratively staying further proceedings in the district court until 5 p.m. (EDT) on August 13, 2026. Epic filed an opposition to the request for an administrative stay, and Apple filed a reply. On August 13, 2026, Justice Kagan denied the stay application.

## What Each Side Argues

### Apple’s arguments

- Apple argues that a court should not be able to hold a party in civil contempt unless the court order clearly and unambiguously prohibits the precise conduct at issue.
- Apple says the Ninth Circuit allowed contempt based on the “spirit” of an injunction, even though the injunction’s text did not address commissions.
- Apple argues that this creates a split among federal appeals courts. Apple says many circuits require a clear and unambiguous order, while the Ninth Circuit allows contempt based on an order’s spirit.
- Apple says fairness requires that people who are ordered by a court to stop doing something must receive explicit notice of what conduct is forbidden before they can be punished for violating the order.
- Apple points to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 65, which it says requires specificity in injunctions to ensure clear notice.
- Apple argues that contempt is a serious power and should not be based on an open-ended inquiry into what a court might have intended beyond the order’s words.
- Apple also argued in its petition that the Ninth Circuit upheld a broad injunction affecting millions of developers who were not parties to Epic’s case. But the Supreme Court granted review only on the civil contempt question, not this second question.

### Epic’s arguments

- Epic argues that a party can be held in contempt not only when the exact words of an injunction prohibit the conduct, but also when a reasonable person reading the injunction’s terms in light of its context and purpose would understand the conduct to be prohibited.
- Epic says courts should be able to prevent parties from circumventing an injunction — that is, getting around the order by using alternative methods.
- Epic argues that Apple knew what the injunction was meant to accomplish: allowing linked-out purchases so consumers could choose other payment systems and price competition could occur.
- Epic says Apple imposed a commission on linked-out purchases at a rate so high that developers would lose money if consumers used a payment system other than Apple’s.
- Epic also says Apple imposed design restrictions that made it harder for users to use other payment systems.
- Epic argues that Apple’s knowledge and bad faith — meaning dishonest intent or awareness that it was violating the order — support the contempt finding.
- Epic says the Supreme Court should affirm the contempt ruling, but if the Court disagrees with the legal standard, it should send the case back to the lower courts to apply the correct law to the facts.

## Where the Case Stands

The docket shows the following steps:

- May 21, 2026: Apple filed its petition for a writ of certiorari, asking the Supreme Court to review the Ninth Circuit’s decision.
- June 4, 2026: Epic filed a brief in opposition. A brief is a written legal argument filed with the Court.
